title: Foreign Investors Pulled ₹21,745 Crore From Indian Stocks in Late September
excerpt: Foreign portfolio investors sold ₹21,745 crore ($2.3 billion) of Indian equities in the second half of September, intensifying a selloff led by financials, oil & gas, and auto stocks as rising US yields and crude prices drove a global allocation reset.
body:
• FPIs sold ₹21,745 crore of Indian equities during September 16–30, after selling ₹14,116 crore in the first half — a full-month outflow of roughly ₹35,860 crore, the largest since April.
  • Financial stocks took the biggest hit at ₹6,943 crore in the fortnight, followed by oil & gas (₹4,469 crore) and autos (₹3,542 crore); telecom, metals, consumer durables, and capital goods also saw outflows.
  • The drivers are largely global: US 10-year yields near 5.3%, Brent crude around $102 a barrel, a weak rupee at 96.31 per dollar, and rotation toward AI-led North Asian markets.
  • What it means for investors: domestic institutions absorbed far more than foreigners sold — DIIs bought ₹76,030 crore of equities in September per provisional NSE data, with SIP flows staying steady. Eight straight weeks of declines have made large-cap valuations attractive; the signal from strategists is selective entry, not exit.

Foreign portfolio investors stepped up selling of Indian equities in the second half of September, with financial, oil & gas, auto, telecom, and metal stocks bearing the brunt of the outflows. FPIs sold ₹21,745 crore (about $2.3 billion) during September 16–30, after selling ₹14,116 crore in the first half of the month, according to The Economic Times.

The fortnight capped a volatile month: the Nifty 50 fell about 6.4% in September and the Sensex about 6.2%. The rupee slid to 96.31 per dollar, a two-month low, while Brent crude climbed to roughly $102 a barrel — up about 7% in a month.

The September unwind, in numbers

September reversed the summer's relief rally: FPIs had bought ₹20,200 crore of equities in July and ₹29,630 crore in August, but September's ₹35,860 crore outflow erased both. Selling continued into October, with ₹9,232 crore withdrawn on October 1 alone, per CDSL data reported by The Daily Jagran.

For the fiscal first half the damage runs deeper: FPIs pulled ₹1.29 lakh crore from equities between April and mid-September, financials (₹47,030 crore) and oil & gas (₹33,359 crore) leading, per Prime Database analysis. Year-to-date 2026 outflows stand at roughly ₹2.7 lakh crore — well above the ₹1.66 lakh crore withdrawn in all of 2025.

It is not one-way traffic: healthcare attracted ₹2,114 crore of FPI buying in the September 1–15 fortnight, its sixth straight, and FPIs invested ₹9,676 crore through the primary market in September — foreign capital is getting more selective, not abandoning India.

Valuations, yields and crude — the forces behind the exit

Vishad Turakhia, CEO of Equirus Securities, told The Economic Times the selling reflects "a combination of portfolio rebalancing, profit-taking and a greater focus on valuations relative to earnings growth," adding that financials — which dominate foreign India portfolios — tend to take the biggest hit when overseas investors cut exposure.

Three global pressures converged in September. US 10-year Treasury yields climbed to around 5.3%, their highest in over two decades, resetting the hurdle rate for emerging-market allocations. Elevated crude prices, amplified by Hormuz-related supply risks, raised India's import bill and inflation risk. A weakening rupee eroded dollar returns for foreign funds.

Rajesh Singla, CEO at Alpha AMC, called it "a global allocation story, not a domestic earnings one," citing profit-booking after the July–August inflows and rotation toward AI-led North Asian markets. Geojit's VK Vijayakumar added that a poor monsoon — 13% below normal — weighed on sentiment.

Policy is now leaning the same way as the pressure. On October 8, the Reserve Bank of India raised the repo rate to 5.50% — its first rate hike in nearly four years — and shifted its stance to "calibrated tightening," India Today reported, underscoring that the central bank is prioritizing price stability over growth support.

Within telecom there is a stock-specific wrinkle: with Jio Platforms' IPO approaching, some investors appear to be trimming Bharti Airtel to deploy into the listing, analysts told ET.

What it means for portfolios

The offset is domestic: DIIs bought a provisional ₹76,030 crore of cash equities in September — more than foreigners sold — extending a 38-month buying streak. Sustained SIP flows are absorbing much of the foreign exit, and SME and small-cap segments with limited FPI ownership remain relatively insulated.

For long-horizon investors, the reset has useful consequences. Vijayakumar said the correction has made large-cap valuations attractive after eight straight weeks of losses. The strategists' message: the selling is a rotation, not an exodus — Choice Wealth's Dheeraj Gaur said foreign investors are becoming "much more selective about where they deploy capital," favoring quality large-caps over frothy segments.

What to watch

Whether the cycle ends now hinges on the variables that started it: falling crude and US bond yields would be the clearest reversal trigger, analysts say. Until then, FPI flows, the rupee's trajectory, and the RBI's new tightening stance will set the tone for Indian equities in the final quarter of 2026.
